metadata.title: Preparing for Life in a Digital Age

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: ICILS 2013 uses a multistage clustered sampling design with students nested within schools and education systems. In the multilevel regression analyses, the authors report that they obtained estimates after applying sampling weights at the student and school levels (and used MPlus for estimation). The chapter also describes that missing data were handled by excluding students with no student questionnaire data and imputing missing school/teacher questionnaire-derived variables using national mean/median values plus missing indicators. For analysts using ICILS microdata, the intended approach is to apply the provided sampling weights to obtain population-representative estimates and to respect the multilevel structure (students within schools).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This chapter reports ICILS CIL achievement using an IRT/Rasch-based scaling approach and multilevel regression modeling of scale scores, rather than a PV-based achievement framework. Plausible values handling is therefore not applicable to the reported modeling outputs in this text. Missing data handling is described qualitatively (exclusion of students with no student questionnaire data; mean/median imputation for some school/teacher variables with missing indicators), but the chapter does not specify a PV-imputation or PV-combining procedure, so a PV-specific missing-data handling label cannot be mapped precisely.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The chapter analyzes ICILS 2013 student data for Grade 8 CIL. In multivariate analyses, the authors excluded students with no student questionnaire data, which was possible because missingness for student-level variables was small. For variables derived from the ICT-coordinator questionnaire (school ICT resources and school ICT experience) and from the teacher survey, missing values were treated by setting them to national mean or median values and adding missing-indicator variables for missing school and missing teacher data. They also excluded some countries/benchmarking participants with insufficient data, including the City of Buenos Aires (Argentina) and Switzerland due to low teacher-survey participation, and excluded the Netherlands due to missing parental occupation information needed to derive the socioeconomic composite index. Overall, about 97% of tested students were included in the analysis, with Germany somewhat lower (93%).

data.outcome_summary: This chapter is part of the ICILS 2013 international report on students’ Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) and related school/teacher contexts. CIL achievement is measured with a computer-based assessment comprising four thematic modules of discrete tasks plus a large open task (e.g., creating a poster), mapped onto a CIL scale with proficiency levels. The chapter reports cross-country distributions of CIL scores (country means spanning roughly 361 to 553 scale points) and describes how student access, familiarity, and learning experiences relate to CIL. For multivariate analyses, the authors estimate two-level hierarchical models (students nested within schools) using MPlus and apply sampling weights at student and school levels. Missing data are handled by excluding students with no student questionnaire data and imputing missing school/teacher-derived variables using national mean/median values with missing indicators. The chapter emphasizes that ICT resources matter partly through socioeconomic context, while students’ experience and regular use of computers show more robust associations with CIL.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction corresponds to an IEA/OECD-style large-scale assessment report chapter rather than an ML predictive paper. The text focuses on assessment design, scaling, descriptive comparisons, and multilevel regression associations rather than training/evaluating machine learning models. Consequently, fields related to ML techniques and structured predictive findings are intentionally left empty, and plausible-values handling is not applicable to the reported scaling/modeling outputs in this chapter.
